purpose: Denosumab is used to strengthen bones and reduce the risk of fractures in people with osteoporosis or certain cancers that affect the bones. It is also used to prevent bone loss in people receiving hormone-blocking cancer treatments. In higher doses (Xgeva), it helps protect bones in patients with bone metastases or a rare bone tumor called giant cell tumor of bone.
how_it_works: Your body has a natural process where old bone is broken down and new bone is built up. Denosumab works by blocking a protein called RANK ligand, which is responsible for triggering bone breakdown. By blocking this protein, the medication slows down bone loss and helps keep your bones stronger and denser over time.
common_side_effects: Back pain, joint or muscle pain, low calcium levels in the blood (which can cause muscle cramps or tingling), infections such as bladder or skin infections, and fatigue. Some people also experience nausea or headache.
warnings: This medication can cause dangerously low calcium levels, so it is very important to take calcium and vitamin D supplements as directed by your doctor. A rare but serious side effect called osteonecrosis of the jaw (jaw bone problems) can occur, so good dental hygiene and telling your dentist you take this medication is very important. Another rare side effect is unusual fractures of the thigh bone. Do not stop taking this medication without talking to your doctor, as stopping suddenly can increase your risk of spine fractures.
typical_dosing: For osteoporosis (Prolia): one injection of 60 mg given under the skin every 6 months, administered by a healthcare provider. For cancer-related bone conditions (Xgeva): 120 mg injection given under the skin once every 4 weeks, with extra doses sometimes given in the first month. Your doctor will decide which dose and schedule is right for you.
